docs.title: Welcome to Lazy Predict
docs.text: Lazy Predict helps you build and benchmark a large number of machine learning models with minimal code, so you can quickly discover which algorithms work best on your dataset — without any parameter tuning.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
ClassificationRegressionTime Series 
from lazypredict.Supervised import LazyClassifier
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

data = load_breast_cancer()
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    data.data, data.target, test_size=0.2, random_state=42
)

clf = LazyClassifier(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)
print(models)

from lazypredict.Supervised import LazyRegressor
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

data = load_diabetes()
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    data.data, data.target, test_size=0.2, random_state=42
)

reg = LazyRegressor(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
models, predictions = reg.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)
print(models)

import numpy as np
from lazypredict.TimeSeriesForecasting import LazyForecaster

t = np.arange(200)
y = 10 + 0.05 * t + 3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 12) + np.random.normal(0, 1, 200)

fcst = LazyForecaster(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y[:180], y[180:])
print(scores)

docs.title: Feature Highlights
docs.text:
• Zero-boilerplate benchmarking — one call trains and evaluates all models
  • 40+ classifiers and regressors from scikit-learn plus optional boosting libraries
  • 20+ time series forecasting models — Naive, ETS, ARIMA, Theta, ML, LSTM/GRU, TimesFM
  • GPU acceleration — XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, cuML (RAPIDS), LSTM/GRU, TimesFM
  • Automatic seasonal period detection via autocorrelation analysis
  • Exogenous variables support in time series forecasting (SARIMAX, AutoARIMA, ML models)
  • Multiple categorical encoders — OneHot, Ordinal, Target, Binary
  • MLflow integration — automatic experiment tracking via environment variable
  • Cross-validation — both train/test split and k-fold CV supported
  • Per-model timeout — skip slow models automatically
  • Hyperparameter tuning — Optuna, scikit-learn, or FLAML backends
  • Explainability — permutation importance and optional SHAP values
  • Ensemble methods — simple average, weighted average, stacking
  • Visualization — forecast plots, model comparison, residuals, error heatmaps
  • Intel Extension acceleration — opt-in CPU speedup via sklearnex.patch_sklearn()
  • Python 3.10 – 3.14 support
  • MIT licensed, free software

docs.title: Hyperparameter Tuning
docs.text: After benchmarking, automatically tune the top-k models using Optuna, scikit-learn, or FLAML.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install lazypredict[tune]    # Optuna (default)
pip install lazypredict[flaml]   # FLAML alternative

docs.title: Supervised Models
docs.text:
from lazypredict.Supervised import LazyClassifier

clf = LazyClassifier(
    verbose=1,
    tune=True,
    tune_top_k=5,          # tune the 5 best models
    tune_trials=50,         # 50 Optuna trials per model
    tune_timeout=120,       # max 2 minutes per model (no new trial starts after it)
    tune_backend="optuna",  # "optuna", "sklearn", or "flaml"
)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

# One row per tuned model: "Best Score" (mean cross-validated score on the
# training data, higher is better), "Best Params" (a dict) and "Status"
print(clf.tuned_scores_)

# Models whose tuning succeeded: best hyperparameters and the pipeline refitted with them
for name, pipeline in clf.tuned_models_.items():
    print(name, clf.tuned_params_[name])

# predict() and explain() use the tuned models with tuned=True, and convert
# NumPy input to the training columns as for the benchmarked models
clf.predict(X_test, tuned=True)
clf.explain(X_test, y_test, tuned=True)

Tuning is reproducible for a given random_state, uses cv folds (5 when cv is not set), and a model that cannot be tuned is reported in the Status column instead of aborting the others. Models without a search space (for example LassoCV, which tunes its own regularisation) are listed as "no search space".

docs.title: Time Series
docs.text:
from lazypredict.TimeSeriesForecasting import LazyForecaster

fcst = LazyForecaster(
    tune=True,
    tune_top_k=3,
    tune_trials=30,
    tune_metric="RMSE",     # "RMSE", "MAE", "MAPE", "SMAPE", "MASE"
    tune_seasonal=False,    # also search over seasonal_period
)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)

# "Best RMSE" (mean temporal-CV error, lower is better), "Best Params", "Status"
print(fcst.tuned_scores_)
fcst.tuned_models_   # {name: forecaster refitted with the best parameters} for the tuned models

docs.title: Using the Tuning API Directly
docs.text:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

from lazypredict.preprocessing import build_preprocessor, prepare_dataframes
from lazypredict.tuning import tune_supervised_optuna

X_train_df, X_test_df = prepare_dataframes(X_train, X_test)
preprocessor = build_preprocessor(X_train_df, categorical_encoder="onehot")

best_params, best_score = tune_supervised_optuna(
    "RandomForestClassifier",
    RandomForestClassifier,
    X_train_df,
    y_train,
    preprocessor,
    scoring="balanced_accuracy",
    cv=5,
    n_trials=100,
)

tune_supervised_sklearn (RandomizedSearchCV) and tune_supervised_flaml take the same leading arguments.

docs.title: Explainability
docs.text: Compute feature importance for all benchmarked models.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install lazypredict[explain]    # SHAP
pip install lazypredict[interpret]  # InterpretML (EBM)

docs.title: Permutation Importance (no extra dependencies)
docs.text:
from lazypredict.Supervised import LazyRegressor

reg = LazyRegressor(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
models, predictions = reg.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

# Features as rows, models as columns
importance_df = reg.explain(X_test, y_test, method="permutation", n_repeats=10)
print(importance_df)

docs.title: SHAP Values
docs.text:
# {model name: SHAP values for the transformed features}
shap_values = reg.explain(X_test, y_test, method="shap", max_samples=100)
shap_values["RandomForestRegressor"].shape   # (n_samples, n_features)

Binary classifiers return the values of the positive class; multiclass classifiers return an array of shape (n_samples, n_features, n_classes). The lower-level lazypredict.explainability.explain_shap(models, X_test, step_name="regressor") takes the dict of fitted pipelines (reg.models).

docs.title: InterpretML (EBM)
docs.text: When interpret is installed, ExplainableBoostingClassifier and ExplainableBoostingRegressor are automatically included in benchmarking. These are inherently interpretable glass-box models.

docs.title: Time Series Visualization
docs.text: Requires pip install lazypredict[viz].

docs.title: Via LazyForecaster.plot_results()
docs.text:
fcst = LazyForecaster(predictions=True, verbose=0)
scores, pred_df = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)

# Overlay all model forecasts on actual series
fig = fcst.plot_results(plot_type="forecast")

# Bar chart ranking models by a metric
fig = fcst.plot_results(plot_type="comparison", metric="MAE", top_k=10)

# Residual diagnostics (ACF, histogram, Q-Q)
fig = fcst.plot_results(plot_type="residuals", model_name="Ridge_TS")

# Violin plot of absolute errors per model
fig = fcst.plot_results(plot_type="errors")

# Heatmap of all metrics × all models
fig = fcst.plot_results(plot_type="heatmap")

docs.title: Direct Plotting Functions
docs.text:
from lazypredict.ts_visualization import (
    plot_forecast,
    plot_model_comparison,
    plot_residuals,
    plot_error_distribution,
    plot_metrics_heatmap,
)

# Forecast overlay

# Model comparison bar chart
fig = plot_model_comparison(scores, metric="RMSE", top_k=10)

# Residuals for one model
fig = plot_residuals(y_test, y_pred, model_name="Ridge_TS", seasonal_period=12)

# Error distribution
fig = plot_error_distribution(y_test, predictions_dict)

# Metrics heatmap
fig = plot_metrics_heatmap(scores)

docs.title: Ensemble Methods
docs.text: Combine predictions from multiple models after benchmarking.

docs.title: Via LazyForecaster.ensemble()
docs.text:
fcst = LazyForecaster(predictions=True, verbose=0)
scores, pred_df = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)

# Simple average
avg_pred = fcst.ensemble(method="simple_average")

# Inverse-error weighted (lower validation RMSE = higher weight)
weighted_pred = fcst.ensemble(method="weighted_average")

# Stacking (Ridge meta-model)
stacked_pred = fcst.ensemble(method="stacking")

Weights and the stacking meta-model are learned on a validation window held out from the end of the training series (each model is refitted on the rest of y_train), never on y_test, so the ensemble can be evaluated on y_test like any single model.

Changed in 0.4.0

ensemble() no longer needs y_true; passing it emits a FutureWarning. Earlier versions fitted the stacking model on y_test, which leaked the test values into the forecast being evaluated.

docs.title: Direct Ensemble Functions
docs.text:
from lazypredict.ensemble import (
    ensemble_simple_average,
    ensemble_weighted_average,
    ensemble_stacking,
)

predictions = {
    "Holt": pred_holt,
    "Ridge_TS": pred_ridge,
    "LSTM_TS": pred_lstm,
}

# Simple average
avg = ensemble_simple_average(predictions)

# Weighted average (lower score = higher weight)
scores_dict = {"Holt": 3.2, "Ridge_TS": 1.8, "LSTM_TS": 2.5}
weighted = ensemble_weighted_average(predictions, scores=scores_dict)

# Stacking: fit the meta-model on the same models' forecasts of a
# validation period (val_predictions vs. y_val), then apply it to the
# forecasts being combined
stacked = ensemble_stacking(val_predictions, y_true=y_val, pred_test=predictions)

docs.title: Horizon Strategies
docs.text:
Control how ML models generate multi-step forecasts.

from lazypredict.TimeSeriesForecasting import LazyForecaster

# Recursive (default): single model, autoregressively predicts one step at a time
fcst = LazyForecaster(horizon_strategy="recursive")

# Direct: one separate model trained per forecast horizon step
# More accurate for longer horizons but slower
fcst = LazyForecaster(horizon_strategy="direct")

# Multi-output: MultiOutputRegressor wrapping a single model
fcst = LazyForecaster(horizon_strategy="multi_output")

Using horizon functions directly:

from lazypredict.horizon import direct_forecast, multi_output_forecast
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

# Direct forecasting
y_pred = direct_forecast(
    estimator_class=Ridge,
    y_train=y_train,
    horizon=20,
    n_lags=10,
)

# Multi-output forecasting
y_pred = multi_output_forecast(
    estimator_class=Ridge,
    y_train=y_train,
    horizon=20,
    n_lags=10,
)

# With exogenous variables, also pass X_exog (training period) and
# X_future (forecast period).

Both raise a ValueError when y_train is too short to train for the requested horizon.

docs.title: Time Series Diagnostics
docs.text:
Check whether a model's residuals look like white noise.

from lazypredict.ts_diagnostics import residual_diagnostics

report = residual_diagnostics(y_test, y_pred, seasonal_period=12)
# dict with: residuals, mean, std, ljung_box_stat, ljung_box_pvalue,
# jarque_bera_stat, jarque_bera_pvalue, acf_values, is_white_noise, is_normal

# Or for every fitted forecaster at once:
diagnostics_df = fcst.diagnose()

docs.title: Auto-convert PySpark/Dask DataFrames
docs.text:
Lazy Predict automatically converts PySpark and Dask DataFrames to pandas when they are passed to fit():

# PySpark DataFrame — automatically collected to the driver
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()
sdf = spark.createDataFrame(df)

clf = LazyClassifier(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
models, predictions = clf.fit(sdf_train, sdf_test, y_train, y_test)

You can also convert explicitly:

from lazypredict.distributed import auto_convert_dataframe

pandas_df = auto_convert_dataframe(spark_df, name="X_train")

docs.title: Spark MLlib Integration
docs.text: Benchmark PySpark MLlib models on large distributed datasets.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: pip install lazypredict[spark]

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from lazypredict.spark import LazySparkClassifier, LazySparkRegressor

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("LazyPredict").getOrCreate()

# Load data as a Spark DataFrame
train_df = spark.read.csv("train.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)
test_df = spark.read.csv("test.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)

feature_cols = [c for c in train_df.columns if c != "label"]

clf = LazySparkClassifier(verbose=1, ignore_warnings=True, label_col="label")
scores = clf.fit(train_df, test_df, feature_cols=feature_cols)
print(scores)

Supported Spark MLlib models:

Classifiers: LogisticRegression, RandomForestClassifier, GBTClassifier, DecisionTreeClassifier, LinearSVC, NaiveBayes

Regressors: LinearRegression, RandomForestRegressor, GBTRegressor, DecisionTreeRegressor, GeneralizedLinearRegression

docs.title: Time Series Tuning
docs.text:
Tune hyperparameters of time series forecasting models directly:

from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

from lazypredict.TimeSeriesForecasting import MLForecaster
from lazypredict.ts_tuning import tune_forecaster_optuna

# Tune a specific forecaster wrapper with expanding-window CV on y_train
best_params, best_score = tune_forecaster_optuna(
    "Ridge_TS",
    MLForecaster(Ridge, "Ridge_TS"),
    y_train,
    X_train=None,
    seasonal_period=12,
    tune_metric="RMSE",
    cv=3,
    n_trials=50,
    timeout=60,
)
print(f"Best params: {best_params}, Best RMSE: {best_score:.4f}")

docs.title: title: Contributing
docs.text:
Contributions are welcome, and they are greatly appreciated! Every little bit helps, and credit will always be given.

You can contribute in many ways:

docs.title: Report Bugs
docs.text:
Report bugs at https://github.com/shankarpandala/lazypredict/issues.

If you are reporting a bug, please include:

  • Your operating system name and version.
  • Your Python version and virtual environment details.
  • Any details about your local setup that might be helpful in troubleshooting.
  • Detailed steps to reproduce the bug.

docs.title: Fix Bugs
docs.text: Look through the GitHub issues for bugs. Anything tagged with "bug" and "help wanted" is open to whoever wants to implement it.

docs.title: Submit Feedback

The best way to send feedback is to file an issue at https://github.com/shankarpandala/lazypredict/issues.

If you are proposing a feature:

  • Explain in detail how it would work.
  • Keep the scope as narrow as possible, to make it easier to implement.
  • Remember that this is a volunteer-driven project, and that contributions are welcome.

docs.title: Get Started!
docs.text:
Ready to contribute? Here's how to set up lazypredict for local development.

  1. Fork the lazypredict repo on GitHub.

  2. Clone your fork locally:

    git clone git@github.com:your_name_here/lazypredict.git

  3. Install your local copy into a virtual environment:

    cd lazypredict/
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate   # On Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"

  4. Create a branch for local development:

    git checkout -b name-of-your-bugfix-or-feature

    Now you can make your changes locally.

  5. When you're done making changes, check that your changes pass flake8 and the tests:

    flake8 lazypredict tests
pytest

    You can also run the test suite on every supported Python version with tox:

    pip install tox
tox

  6. Commit your changes and push your branch to GitHub:

    git add .
git commit -m "Your detailed description of your changes."
git push origin name-of-your-bugfix-or-feature

  7. Submit a pull request through the GitHub website.

docs.title: Pull Request Guidelines
docs.text:
Before you submit a pull request, check that it meets these guidelines:

  1. The pull request should include tests.
  2. If the pull request adds functionality, the docs should be updated. Put your new functionality into a function with a docstring, and add the feature to the list in README.md.
  3. The pull request should work for Python 3.10 through 3.14. GitHub Actions CI will automatically run the tests for all supported Python versions.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
To run a subset of tests:

pytest tests/test_supervised.py

To run tests with coverage:

pytest --cov=lazypredict --cov-report=term-missing

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Releases are cut from dev and published to PyPI by .github/workflows/publish.yml, which runs when a GitHub release is published (pushing a tag on its own does not publish anything).

  1. Bump the version. lazypredict/__init__.py is the single source of truth (pyproject.toml reads it); recipe/meta.yaml, CITATION.cff and .bumpversion.cfg must carry the same string, which tests/test_version.py enforces:

    pip install bump-my-version
bump-my-version bump minor        # or: patch / major

    For a pre-release, pass the exact version instead, e.g. bump-my-version bump --new-version 0.5.0a1; bump-my-version bump pre_n then goes to 0.5.0a2, and --new-version 0.5.0 finalizes it.

  2. Move the "Unreleased" notes in HISTORY.md under the new version and update date-released in CITATION.cff.

  3. Open a pull request into dev, wait for CI to pass, and merge it.

  4. On GitHub, draft a new release on the merged commit with tag v<version> (for example v0.4.0; tick "Set as a pre-release" for a/b/rc versions) and publish it.

The publish workflow first checks that the tag matches lazypredict.__version__ and fails before building anything if it does not, then runs the tests, builds the sdist and wheel, smoke-tests the wheel, uploads them to PyPI via Trusted Publishing and attaches them to the GitHub release. If an upload fails for a transient reason, re-run it from the Actions tab (Publish to PyPI > Run workflow, entering the tag).

Instead of step 4 you can push an annotated tag on the merged commit and run the workflow manually for it:

git tag -a v0.4.0 -m "0.4.0" && git push origin v0.4.0
gh workflow run publish.yml --ref v0.4.0 -f tag=v0.4.0

The workflow then creates the GitHub release, with generated notes, after the upload to PyPI has succeeded.

The conda-forge feedstock picks up new PyPI releases automatically through the conda-forge autotick bot; recipe/meta.yaml is only used by CI to check that the package still builds with conda.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: This page contains detailed examples of how to use Lazy Predict in various scenarios.

docs.title: Basic Classification
docs.text:
Here's a basic example using the breast cancer dataset:

from lazypredict.Supervised import LazyClassifier
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Load data
data = load_breast_cancer()
X = data.data
y = data.target

# Split data
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=123)

# Create classifier
clf = LazyClassifier(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True, custom_metric=None)

# Fit and get models
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)
print(models)

docs.title: Classification with Custom Metric
docs.text:
You can use custom metrics for model evaluation:

from sklearn.metrics import f1_score

def custom_f1(y_true, y_pred):
    return f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average='weighted')

clf = LazyClassifier(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True, custom_metric=custom_f1)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

docs.title: Advanced Classification Options
docs.text:
Use advanced options like categorical encoding, timeout, and cross-validation:

clf = LazyClassifier(
    verbose=1,                          # Show progress
    ignore_warnings=True,               # Suppress warnings
    custom_metric=None,                 # Use default metrics
    predictions=True,                   # Return predictions
    classifiers='all',                  # Use all available classifiers
    categorical_encoder='onehot',       # Encoding strategy
    timeout=60,                         # Max time per model in seconds
    cv=5                                # Cross-validation folds
)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

docs.title: Basic Regression
docs.text:
Here's an example using the diabetes dataset:

from lazypredict.Supervised import LazyRegressor
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Load data
diabetes = load_diabetes()
X = diabetes.data
y = diabetes.target

# Split data
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=123)

# Create and fit regressor
reg = LazyRegressor(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True, custom_metric=None)
models, predictions = reg.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)
print(models)

docs.title: Working with Pandas DataFrames
docs.text:
Lazy Predict works seamlessly with pandas DataFrames:

import pandas as pd

# Your DataFrame
df = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=diabetes.feature_names)

# Split features and target
X = df
y = pd.Series(diabetes.target)

# Rest remains the same
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)
reg = LazyRegressor(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
models, predictions = reg.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

docs.title: Categorical Feature Encoding
docs.text: Lazy Predict supports multiple categorical encoding strategies:

docs.title: OneHot Encoding (Default)
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
from lazypredict.Supervised import LazyClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Load data with categorical features
df = pd.read_csv('data_with_categories.csv')
X = df.drop('target', axis=1)
y = df['target']

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3)

# Default onehot encoding
clf = LazyClassifier(categorical_encoder='onehot', verbose=0)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

docs.title: Ordinal Encoding
docs.text:
Useful for ordered categorical features or when one-hot encoding creates too many features:

clf = LazyClassifier(categorical_encoder='ordinal', verbose=0)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

docs.title: Target Encoding
docs.text:
Target encoding requires the category-encoders package:

pip install category-encoders

clf = LazyClassifier(categorical_encoder='target', verbose=0)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

docs.title: Binary Encoding
docs.text:
Binary encoding is efficient for high-cardinality features:

# Requires category-encoders package
clf = LazyClassifier(categorical_encoder='binary', verbose=0)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

docs.title: Comparing Encoders
docs.text:
import pandas as pd

results = {}
for encoder in ['onehot', 'ordinal', 'target', 'binary']:
    try:
        clf = LazyClassifier(
            categorical_encoder=encoder,
            verbose=0,
            ignore_warnings=True
        )
        models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)
        results[encoder] = models.head(3)
        print(f"\n{encoder.upper()} Encoding Results:")
        print(models.head(3))
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"{encoder}: {e}")

docs.title: Using with MLflow
docs.text:
Lazy Predict has built-in MLflow integration for experiment tracking. You can enable it by setting the MLflow tracking URI:

import os
os.environ['MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI'] = 'sqlite:///mlflow.db'  # Local SQLite tracking
# Or for remote tracking:
# os.environ['MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI'] = 'http://your-mlflow-server:5000'

# MLflow tracking will be automatically enabled
reg = LazyRegressor(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
models, predictions = reg.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

The following metrics and artifacts will be automatically logged to MLflow:

  • Model metrics (R-squared, RMSE, etc.)
  • Training time
  • The model name and the estimator's hyperparameters
  • Model signatures
  • A custom metric, as custom_metric (if provided)
  • Model artifacts for each trained model (not registered in the model registry)

You can view the results in the MLflow UI:

mlflow ui

docs.title: For Databricks Users
docs.text:
If you're using Databricks, MLflow tracking is automatically configured:

# MLflow tracking will use Databricks tracking URI automatically
reg = LazyRegressor(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
models, predictions = reg.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

docs.title: Getting Model Objects
docs.text:
You can access the trained model objects:

# Get all trained models
model_dictionary = reg.provide_models(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

# Access specific model
random_forest = model_dictionary['RandomForestRegressor']

# Make predictions with a specific model. The pipelines expect a DataFrame with
# the training columns; reg.predict() also converts NumPy input for you.
predictions = reg.predict(X_test)["RandomForestRegressor"]

docs.title: Model Timeout
docs.text:
Set a maximum time limit for each model to prevent long-running models from blocking:

# Limit each model to 60 seconds
clf = LazyClassifier(timeout=60, verbose=1)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

# Models that exceed the timeout will be skipped
# Check for skipped models in the verbose output

This is particularly useful when:

  • Working with large datasets where some models might take very long
  • Running experiments with time constraints
  • Preventing specific slow models from blocking the entire pipeline

docs.title: GPU Acceleration
docs.text:
Lazy Predict supports GPU acceleration for models that support it. Enable GPU with the use_gpu=True parameter:

from lazypredict.Supervised import LazyClassifier, LazyRegressor

# Classification with GPU
clf = LazyClassifier(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True, use_gpu=True)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

# Regression with GPU
reg = LazyRegressor(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True, use_gpu=True)
models, predictions = reg.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

Supported GPU backends:

  • XGBoost — uses device="cuda"
  • LightGBM — uses device="gpu"
  • CatBoost — uses task_type="GPU"
  • cuML (RAPIDS) — GPU-native scikit-learn replacements added automatically
  • LSTM / GRU — PyTorch models use CUDA device
  • TimesFM — placed on CUDA device for inference

docs.title: cuML (RAPIDS) GPU Acceleration
docs.text:
When cuML is installed and use_gpu=True, GPU-accelerated versions of common scikit-learn models are automatically added to the benchmark:

# Install cuML (requires NVIDIA GPU + CUDA)
pip install cuml-cu12  # for CUDA 12

# cuML models are added automatically when use_gpu=True
clf = LazyClassifier(use_gpu=True, verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)
# Results will include cuML_LogisticRegression, cuML_RandomForestClassifier, etc.

cuML GPU models added:

  • Classifiers: LogisticRegression, RandomForestClassifier, KNeighborsClassifier, SVC
  • Regressors: LinearRegression, Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet, RandomForestRegressor, KNeighborsRegressor, SVR

docs.title: Time Series Forecasting with GPU
docs.text:
from lazypredict.TimeSeriesForecasting import LazyForecaster

fcst = LazyForecaster(
    verbose=0,
    ignore_warnings=True,
    use_gpu=True,       # GPU for XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, LSTM, GRU, TimesFM
)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)

Note

GPU acceleration requires a CUDA-capable GPU and PyTorch installed with CUDA support. If CUDA is not available, models automatically fall back to CPU with a warning.

docs.title: Using Local Foundation Model Weights
docs.text:
If you are offline, behind a firewall, or in an air-gapped environment, you can point to a local directory containing pre-downloaded model weights instead of downloading from Hugging Face:

from lazypredict.TimeSeriesForecasting import LazyForecaster

fcst = LazyForecaster(
    verbose=0,
    ignore_warnings=True,
    foundation_model_path="/path/to/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch",
)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)

To download the model for later offline use:

# Download once (requires internet)
python -c "
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download
snapshot_download('google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch', local_dir='./timesfm-local')
"

# Then use the local path in air-gapped environments
fcst = LazyForecaster(foundation_model_path="./timesfm-local")

docs.title: Intel Extension Acceleration
docs.text:
For improved performance on Intel CPUs, install Intel Extension for Scikit-learn:

pip install scikit-learn-intelex

Patch scikit-learn before importing lazypredict, so that the accelerated estimators are the ones lazypredict collects:

from sklearnex import patch_sklearn
patch_sklearn()

from lazypredict.Supervised import LazyClassifier

Changed in 0.4.0

Earlier versions called patch_sklearn() automatically on import lazypredict, which changed scikit-learn for the whole Python process. The patch is now opt-in.

docs.title: Basic Forecasting
docs.text:
Benchmark 20+ forecasting models with a single call:

import numpy as np
from lazypredict.TimeSeriesForecasting import LazyForecaster

# Generate sample data with trend + seasonality
np.random.seed(42)
t = np.arange(200)
y = 10 + 0.05 * t + 3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 12) + np.random.normal(0, 1, 200)

y_train, y_test = y[:180], y[180:]

fcst = LazyForecaster(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True, predictions=True)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)
print(scores)

docs.text:
By default the seasonal period is auto-detected via ACF. Override it manually:

fcst = LazyForecaster(
    seasonal_period=12,    # monthly data with yearly cycle
    verbose=0,
    ignore_warnings=True,
)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)

docs.text:
Pass optional exogenous features to models that support them (SARIMAX, AutoARIMA, ML models):

# Create exogenous features
X_train = np.column_stack([np.sin(t[:180]), np.cos(t[:180])])
X_test  = np.column_stack([np.sin(t[180:]), np.cos(t[180:])])

fcst = LazyForecaster(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test, X_train, X_test)

docs.title: Forecasting with Cross-Validation
docs.text:
Use expanding-window time series cross-validation:

fcst = LazyForecaster(
    cv=5,                  # 5-fold TimeSeriesSplit
    verbose=0,
    ignore_warnings=True,
)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)
# scores will contain CV Mean and CV Std columns for each metric

docs.title: Selecting Specific Forecasters
docs.text:
Run only a subset of models:

fcst = LazyForecaster(
    # Holt and AutoARIMA need lazypredict[timeseries], LSTM_TS lazypredict[deeplearning]
    forecasters=["Holt", "AutoARIMA", "Ridge_TS", "LSTM_TS"],
    verbose=0,
    ignore_warnings=True,
)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)

docs.title: Custom Forecasting Metric
docs.text:
Add a custom metric alongside the defaults:

def median_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred):
    return float(np.median(np.abs(y_true - y_pred)))

fcst = LazyForecaster(
    custom_metric=median_absolute_error,
    verbose=0,
    ignore_warnings=True,
)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)
# scores will include a 'median_absolute_error' column

docs.title: Evaluating Results
docs.text:
The scores DataFrame returned by fit() contains:

Column Description MAE Mean Absolute Error RMSE Root Mean Squared Error MAPE Mean Absolute Percentage Error (%) SMAPE Symmetric MAPE (%) MASE Mean Absolute Scaled Error (< 1 beats naive) R-Squared R² coefficient of determination Time Taken Seconds to fit and predict

When cv is set, additional columns appear:

MAE CV Mean, MAE CV Std, RMSE CV Mean, RMSE CV Std, etc.

docs.title: Exogenous Variables
docs.text:
Pass exogenous features to models that support them (SARIMAX, AutoARIMA, ML models):

X_train = np.column_stack([np.sin(t[:180]), np.cos(t[:180])])
X_test  = np.column_stack([np.sin(t[180:]), np.cos(t[180:])])

fcst = LazyForecaster(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test, X_train, X_test)

docs.title: Auto Seasonal Period Detection
docs.text:
By default the seasonal period is auto-detected. The series is detrended, and a lag counts as a season only if:

  • its autocorrelation is a significant peak, measured against the series' short-term autocorrelation;
  • the values grouped by phase (position within the cycle) differ significantly in a one-way ANOVA;
  • that seasonal pattern explains at least 20% of the variance.

The shortest qualifying period wins over its multiples. If the levels show no seasonality, the first differences are searched as well, which finds seasonality on top of a random walk. Series without seasonality (trends, including curved ones, random walks, white noise) are reported as non-seasonal.

Detection needs at least three full cycles of data. For shorter series, or when you know the period, set it explicitly:

fcst = LazyForecaster(seasonal_period=12)   # monthly data with yearly cycle

Set seasonal_period=1 to disable seasonal models.

The exogenous arrays must have one row per value of y_train / y_test, and X_train and X_test must be passed together; targets with missing values are rejected, so fill or drop them first.

docs.title: Cross-Validation
docs.text:
Use TimeSeriesSplit expanding-window cross-validation:

fcst = LazyForecaster(cv=5, verbose=0)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)
# scores includes "MAE CV Mean", "RMSE CV Mean", etc.

docs.title: Selecting Specific Models
docs.text:
Run only a subset of models by name:

fcst = LazyForecaster(
    # Holt and AutoARIMA need lazypredict[timeseries], LSTM_TS lazypredict[deeplearning]
    forecasters=["Naive", "Holt", "AutoARIMA", "Ridge_TS", "LSTM_TS"],
    verbose=0,
)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)

docs.title: Custom Metric
docs.text:
def median_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred):
    return float(np.median(np.abs(np.asarray(y_true) - np.asarray(y_pred))))

fcst = LazyForecaster(custom_metric=median_absolute_error, verbose=0)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)
# scores includes a "median_absolute_error" column

docs.title: Horizon Strategies for ML Models
docs.text:
Control how ML models forecast multiple steps ahead:

# Recursive (default): single model, autoregressively forecasts step by step
fcst = LazyForecaster(horizon_strategy="recursive")

# Direct: one model per horizon step (more accurate for longer horizons)
fcst = LazyForecaster(horizon_strategy="direct")

# Multi-output: MultiOutputRegressor wrapper
fcst = LazyForecaster(horizon_strategy="multi_output")

docs.title: Ensemble Predictions
docs.text:
After calling fit() with predictions=True, combine model predictions:

fcst = LazyForecaster(predictions=True, verbose=0)
scores, pred_df = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)

# Simple average of all model predictions
avg = fcst.ensemble(method="simple_average")

# Inverse-error weighted average (lower validation RMSE = higher weight)
weighted = fcst.ensemble(method="weighted_average")

# Stacking (Ridge meta-learner on top)
stacked = fcst.ensemble(method="stacking")

Weights and the stacking meta-model are learned on a validation window held out from the end of y_train, so y_test stays untouched for evaluation. (y_true= is no longer needed and emits a FutureWarning.)

docs.title: Saving and Loading Models
docs.text:
# Save fitted models to disk
fcst.save_models("./my_forecasters")

# Load in a new session
fcst2 = LazyForecaster()
fcst2.load_models("./my_forecasters")

# Forecast with loaded models
forecasts = fcst2.predict(y_history=y_train, horizon=20)

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
Requires pip install lazypredict[viz]:

fcst = LazyForecaster(predictions=True, verbose=0)
scores, pred_df = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)

# Plot forecasts vs actuals for all models
fcst.plot_results(y_train=y_train, y_test=y_test, plot_type="forecast")

# Bar chart comparison of model errors
fcst.plot_results(plot_type="comparison", metric="RMSE", top_k=10)

# Residual diagnostics for a single model
fcst.plot_results(plot_type="residuals", model_name="HoltWinters_Add")

# Error distribution violin plot
fcst.plot_results(plot_type="errors")

# Metrics heatmap across all models
fcst.plot_results(plot_type="heatmap")

docs.title: 0.4.1 (unreleased)
docs.text:
• predict() and explain() take tuned=True to use tuned_models_, with the same NumPy-to-DataFrame conversion as the benchmarked models (#631)
  • datetime64 and timedelta64 feature columns are used (as days since 1970 and seconds) instead of being dropped or breaking every model (#632)
  • tune_timeout also limits tune_backend="sklearn": no new candidate starts after it (#632)
  • Seasonal period detection is about 2-3x faster, with identical results (#636, thanks to dexhunter)

The v0.3.1 GitHub release was created on a commit still versioned 0.3.0, so it never reached PyPI. Its changes (documentation on Material for MkDocs and GitHub Pages, the JOSS paper files, the model-name filtering fix and Python 3.14 support) are released as part of 0.4.0.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer is required (3.9 is end-of-life). The minimum versions are now scikit-learn 1.2, pandas 1.5, NumPy 1.23 and click 7.0
  • import lazypredict no longer calls sklearnex.patch_sklearn(). To use scikit-learn-intelex, call patch_sklearn() yourself before importing lazypredict. INTEL_EXTENSION_AVAILABLE only reports whether it is installed
  • Unknown names in classifiers=, regressors= and forecasters= raise a ValueError with a close-match suggestion instead of being ignored, and a single string selects exactly that model
  • LazyClassifier raises a ValueError for continuous targets
  • LazyForecaster.ensemble() no longer needs y_true (passing it emits a FutureWarning); ensemble_stacking() requires pred_test
  • tuned_scores_: "Best Params" holds dicts and a "Status" column reports each model's outcome; the forecaster table's always-NaN "Best Score" column is gone (its score column is "Best ")
  • The MLflow integration no longer calls mlflow.autolog() or registers a model version for every model; each model is logged in a nested run
  • Metrics that cannot be computed are NaN instead of None, so score columns stay numeric

docs.title: Release and packaging
docs.text:
• The publish workflow checks that the release tag matches lazypredict.__version__, runs the tests, smoke-tests the built wheel, can be re-run for an existing tag and attaches the files to the GitHub release. The release-please and auto-release workflows, which could not trigger it, are removed (#577)
  • The conda recipe builds again with conda 26.3.1 and later (#578)
  • PEP 639 license metadata and a single-sourced version; new encoders, test and dev extras replace requirements*.txt; the foundation extra installs timesfm[torch] (#581)
  • CI tests the installed package on Python 3.10 and 3.14 for every pull request, the OS × Python 3.10–3.14 matrix on dev and weekly, and the declared dependency floors; mypy is blocking (#580)
  • The docs preview no longer fails for pull requests from forks, and the API reference renders NumPy-style parameter sections (#579)
  • An optional library that is installed but fails to load, such as XGBoost or LightGBM on macOS without libomp, is skipped with a warning instead of making import lazypredict fail (#611)
  • Merging a pull request no longer cancels the docs deployment, and PR previews are removed when the PR is closed (#612)
  • Running the publish workflow manually for a pushed tag creates the GitHub release once the upload to PyPI has succeeded (#613)

docs.title: Fixes: LazyClassifier and LazyRegressor
docs.text:
• pandas category columns are encoded instead of silently dropped, and string columns no longer rely on deprecated pandas behaviour (#582)
  • Cross-validation metrics for classifiers without predict_proba (#584), and multiclass ROC AUC when the test split lacks a class (#585)
  • fit() starts from a clean state, and every pipeline gets its own preprocessor (#586)
  • Prediction DataFrames keep the index of X_test (#588, contributed by AryanRG in #575)
  • Mixed NumPy/DataFrame inputs to fit(), predict() and explain() (#589)
  • timeout interrupts slow models (on POSIX, in the main thread) and lists them in errors (#590)
  • The CLI exits with status 2 when it fails (#592)
  • tune=True no longer crashes fit(); the scikit-learn backend works for every model with a search space and the FLAML backend for the models FLAML has a learner for; tuning is seeded, uses cv, and exposes tuned_params_ and tuned_models_ (#604, #605)
  • Adjusted R² is NaN instead of dividing by zero or inverting the ranking on small test sets; regressors are ranked by adjusted R², then R² (#606)
  • explain(method="shap") returns SHAP values (#607)
  • MLflow logging works inside an active run (#608)

docs.title: Fixes: LazyForecaster
docs.text:
• Tuned hyperparameters are applied to the refitted models, and tuning is reproducible (#594)
  • The direct and multi-output horizon strategies forecast the right steps; horizon_strategy and n_jobs are honoured (#595)
  • AutoARIMA uses exogenous variables and the seasonal period (#596)
  • Rolling-std features are computed the same way for training and forecasting (#597)
  • Misaligned exogenous data and NaN targets raise errors (#598)
  • predict() accepts exogenous variables (X_history, X_test) and no longer overwrites the fitted models (#599)
  • Seasonal period detection is robust to trends and noise (#600)
  • Weighted-average and stacking ensembles learn from a validation window of the training data instead of the test data (#601)
  • Forecasters are selected by exact name, fit() starts from a clean state, and timeout applies to forecasters (#602)
  • One-column DataFrame targets, functools.partial custom metrics and case-insensitive sort_by work; options are validated (#603)

docs.title: Fixes from the pre-release review
docs.text:
• Holt-Winters models selected by name are skipped with a reason in errors when there is no seasonal period, instead of raising "unknown name" (#615)
  • timeout=float("inf") means no limit, and the SIGALRM handler is always restored (#616); n_jobs=0 is rejected (#617); ensembles work for a one-step test horizon (#618)
  • Seasonal-period detection finds seasonality from three cycles and no longer reports periods for curved trends (#623)
  • The direct and multi-output strategies use every future exogenous row (#624); the stacking ensemble no longer depends on the series' units (#625)
  • Equal numeric category codes match across splits (1 vs 1.0) (#620); object NumPy arrays keep numeric columns numeric, and integer column labels work (#621)
  • The FLAML backend reports defaults as a valid result, keeps CatBoost and LightGBM parameters, and the flaml extra installs flaml[automl] (#622)
  • MLflow tracking problems no longer change benchmark results, and the estimator's hyperparameters are logged (#626)
  • explain(method="shap") explains classifiers through their probabilities (#627)
  • Forecaster tuning works for every horizon strategy and metric (#628)
  • Smaller fixes: one-column targets, DataFrames after a NumPy fit, the CLI exit status and seed, forecast indexes, sort_by validation, the publish workflow's re-runs and smoke test (#619, #629); documentation (#630)

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Fixed examples and API references, regenerated the README result tables and added the missing 0.3.0 changelog entries (#609)
  • YAML issue forms and a pull request template; removed stale planning documents (#610)

• First stable release of the 0.3 series: time series forecasting, hyperparameter tuning, explainability, GPU support and the integrations listed in the pre-release notes below
  • Import torch and timesfm lazily to avoid OpenMP deadlocks with scikit-learn

docs.title: Stable release
docs.text:
Install from PyPI (recommended):

pip install lazypredict

Install from conda-forge:

conda install -c conda-forge lazypredict

docs.title: Core dependencies
docs.text: The base install includes: scikit-learn, pandas, numpy, tqdm, joblib, click.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text: Lazy Predict has several optional dependency groups. Install them with pip extras:

docs.title: Boosting libraries
docs.text:
XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost (all support GPU acceleration):

pip install lazypredict[boost]

On macOS, XGBoost and LightGBM also need the OpenMP runtime:

brew install libomp

Without it, lazypredict warns that the library could not be imported and skips its models.

docs.title: Categorical encoders
docs.text:
Target and binary encoding (categorical_encoder="target" / "binary") via category-encoders:

pip install lazypredict[encoders]

docs.title: Time series forecasting
docs.text:
Statistical models (Holt-Winters, SARIMAX, Theta):

pip install lazypredict[timeseries]

Add deep learning models (LSTM, GRU via PyTorch):

pip install lazypredict[timeseries,deeplearning]

Add the Google TimesFM foundation model (installs timesfm[torch]):

pip install lazypredict[timeseries,foundation]

docs.title: MLflow experiment tracking
docs.text:
pip install lazypredict[mlflow]

Activate tracking by setting an environment variable before running:

import os
os.environ["MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI"] = "sqlite:///mlflow.db"

docs.title: Hyperparameter tuning
docs.text:
pip install lazypredict[tune]      # Optuna backend
pip install lazypredict[flaml]     # FLAML backend

The flaml extra installs flaml[automl], which the FLAML backend needs. Its dependency constraints (at the time of writing, xgboost<3) apply to your environment as well.

Enable with tune=True in any Lazy estimator:

clf = LazyClassifier(tune=True, tune_top_k=5, tune_trials=50)

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
pip install lazypredict[viz]

Required for LazyForecaster.plot_results() and all plotting utilities.

docs.title: Explainability
docs.text:
pip install lazypredict[explain]     # SHAP values
pip install lazypredict[interpret]   # InterpretML (EBM)

docs.title: Distributed / Spark
docs.text: pip install lazypredict[spark]       # PySpark MLlib

docs.title: All optional dependencies
docs.text: pip install lazypredict[all]

docs.title: GPU acceleration
docs.text:
GPU acceleration requires an NVIDIA GPU with CUDA support:

pip install lazypredict[boost]   # XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost (all support GPU)
pip install cuml-cu12            # cuML (RAPIDS) GPU-native sklearn replacements

Enable with use_gpu=True:

clf = LazyClassifier(use_gpu=True)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

Supported GPU backends:

Backend Package Parameter XGBoost xgboost device="cuda" LightGBM lightgbm device="gpu" CatBoost catboost task_type="GPU" cuML cuml-cu12 GPU-native (no extra params) LSTM / GRU torch with CUDA CUDA device TimesFM timesfm CUDA device

All GPU backends fall back to CPU automatically if CUDA is not available.

docs.title: Intel CPU acceleration
docs.text:
For improved performance on Intel CPUs:

pip install scikit-learn-intelex

Patch scikit-learn before importing lazypredict, so that the accelerated estimators are the ones lazypredict collects:

from sklearnex import patch_sklearn
patch_sklearn()

from lazypredict.Supervised import LazyClassifier

Changed in 0.4.0

Earlier versions called patch_sklearn() automatically on import lazypredict, which changed scikit-learn for the whole Python process. The patch is now opt-in.

docs.title: Development install
docs.text:
To set up a local development environment:

git clone https://github.com/shankarpandala/lazypredict
cd lazypredict
pip install -e ".[all,dev]"

Run the tests:

pytest tests/

docs.title: Installing from source (archive)
docs.text:
Download and install without git:

curl -OJL https://github.com/shankarpandala/lazypredict/tarball/master
pip install lazypredict-*.tar.gz

docs.title: Importing
docs.text: import lazypredict

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
Benchmark all available classifiers on a dataset in one call:

from lazypredict.Supervised import LazyClassifier
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

data = load_breast_cancer()
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    data.data, data.target, test_size=0.5, random_state=123
)

clf = LazyClassifier(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True, custom_metric=None)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)
print(models)

The returned models DataFrame is sorted by Balanced Accuracy and includes: Accuracy, Balanced Accuracy, ROC AUC, F1 Score, and Time Taken.

docs.title: Regression
docs.text:
from lazypredict.Supervised import LazyRegressor
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
from sklearn.utils import shuffle
import numpy as np

diabetes = load_diabetes()
X, y = shuffle(diabetes.data, diabetes.target, random_state=13)
X = X.astype(np.float32)
offset = int(X.shape[0] * 0.9)
X_train, y_train = X[:offset], y[:offset]
X_test, y_test = X[offset:], y[offset:]

reg = LazyRegressor(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=False, custom_metric=None)
models, predictions = reg.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)
print(models)

The models DataFrame includes: R-Squared, Adjusted R-Squared, RMSE, and Time Taken.

Deprecated class names

The old Regression and Classification class names are deprecated. Use LazyRegressor and LazyClassifier instead.

docs.title: Time Series Forecasting
docs.text:
LazyForecaster benchmarks 20+ statistical, machine-learning, deep-learning, and foundation models with a single call:

import numpy as np
from lazypredict.TimeSeriesForecasting import LazyForecaster

np.random.seed(42)
t = np.arange(200)
y = 10 + 0.05 * t + 3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 12) + np.random.normal(0, 1, 200)

y_train, y_test = y[:180], y[180:]

fcst = LazyForecaster(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
scores, predictions = fcst.fit(y_train, y_test)
print(scores)

See the Time Series Forecasting page for the full guide.

docs.title: Getting Trained Model Objects
docs.text:
Access the fitted model pipelines after calling fit():

reg = LazyRegressor(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
models, predictions = reg.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

# Predict with one model (NumPy arrays and DataFrames are both accepted)
preds = reg.predict(X_test, model_name="RandomForestRegressor")

# The fitted scikit-learn pipelines (preprocessor + estimator), keyed by name
model_dict = reg.models
rf = model_dict["RandomForestRegressor"]

Each pipeline was fitted on a DataFrame (NumPy input gets the column names feature_0, feature_1, ...), so call reg.predict() rather than the pipeline directly when you have NumPy arrays. Calling fit() again replaces models and errors with the results of the new run.

Pandas category, string and str columns are encoded as categorical features, like object columns. LazyClassifier rejects continuous targets (use LazyRegressor) and warns when an integer target has more distinct values than half the samples.

docs.title: GPU Acceleration
docs.text:
Enable GPU with use_gpu=True:

clf = LazyClassifier(use_gpu=True, verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
models, predictions = clf.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

reg = LazyRegressor(use_gpu=True, verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
models, predictions = reg.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

fcst = LazyForecaster(use_gpu=True, verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)

Supported GPU backends:

  • XGBoost (device="cuda")
  • LightGBM (device="gpu")
  • CatBoost (task_type="GPU")
  • cuML (RAPIDS) — GPU-native sklearn replacements (auto-discovered)
  • LSTM / GRU — PyTorch CUDA
  • TimesFM — PyTorch CUDA

Falls back to CPU automatically if no CUDA GPU is available.

docs.title: Command-Line Interface
docs.text:
Lazy Predict ships a CLI for quick benchmarking from a CSV file:

# Classification
lazypredict --task classification --input data.csv --target label

# Regression
lazypredict --task regression --input data.csv --target price --test-size 0.2

Options:

Flag Description --task classification or regression --input Path to a CSV file --target Column name for the target variable --test-size Fraction for test split (default: 0.2) --random-state Random seed (default: 42) --version Show version --help Show help

The command exits with status 2 (and a message) for a missing option, an unknown target column or an invalid --test-size, so it can be used in scripts.

docs.title: MLflow Integration
docs.text:
Enable automatic experiment tracking by setting MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI before running:

import os
os.environ["MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI"] = "sqlite:///mlflow.db"

reg = LazyRegressor(verbose=0, ignore_warnings=True)
models, predictions = reg.fit(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)
# Metrics and model artifacts are automatically logged to MLflow

Each model is logged as its own run, nested under the active run when you wrap the call in mlflow.start_run(). Fitted pipelines are logged as run artifacts but not registered in the model registry, and mlflow.autolog() is not enabled for you.

View results in the MLflow UI:

mlflow ui

For Databricks, MLflow tracking is configured automatically from the environment.

docs.title: RunTracker
docs.text:
RunTracker(mlflow_module: Any = None)

Best-effort MLflow tracking during one fit().

Tracking never changes the benchmark: the first MLflow error is logged and turns tracking off for the rest of the fit, so an unreachable server or a rejected metric cannot make models fail, and every run that was started is ended exactly once.

Source code in lazypredict/integrations/mlflow.py 
def __init__(self, mlflow_module: Any = None) -> None:
    self._mlflow = mlflow_module
    self.enabled = mlflow_module is not None

docs.title: call
docs.text:
call(function: Callable[..., Any], *args: Any) -> bool

Run one tracking call; False if tracking is off or the call failed.

Source code in lazypredict/integrations/mlflow.py 
def call(self, function: Callable[..., Any], *args: Any) -> bool:
    """Run one tracking call; False if tracking is off or the call failed."""
    if not self.enabled:
        return False
    try:
        function(*args)
    except Exception as exc:
        logger.warning("MLflow tracking failed and is turned off for this fit(): %s", exc)
        self.enabled = False
        return False
    return True

def start(self, run_name: str, **params: Any) -> bool:
    """Start a nested run and log *params*; True if a run was started."""
    if not self.call(start_run, self._mlflow, run_name):
        return False
    for key, value in params.items():
        self.call(self._mlflow.log_param, key, value)
    return True

def setup_mlflow() -> bool:
    """Point MLflow at ``MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI`` when that variable is set.

    Autologging is deliberately not enabled: it is a process-wide setting
    that would change how the user's own code is logged.

    Returns
    -------
    bool
        True if MLflow was successfully configured, False otherwise.
    """
    if is_mlflow_tracking_enabled():
        mlflow.set_tracking_uri(os.environ["MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI"])
        return True
    return False

def log_sklearn_model(
    mlflow_module: Any, model: Any, artifact_name: str, signature: Optional[Any] = None
) -> None:
    """Log *model* as an artifact of the active run without registering it.

    MLflow 3 names the artifact with ``name=``; MLflow 2 only accepts
    ``artifact_path=``.
    """
    log_model = mlflow_module.sklearn.log_model
    key = "name" if "name" in inspect.signature(log_model).parameters else "artifact_path"
    log_model(model, **{key: artifact_name}, signature=signature)

Supervised Models — LazyClassifier and LazyRegressor for rapid model benchmarking.

Provides LazyClassifier and LazyRegressor classes that train multiple scikit-learn models with minimal code to quickly identify which algorithms perform best on a given dataset.

LazyClassifier(verbose: int = 0, ignore_warnings: bool = True, custom_metric: Optional[Callable] = None, predictions: bool = False, random_state: int = 42, classifiers: Union[str, List] = 'all', cv: Optional[int] = None, timeout: Optional[Union[int, float]] = None, categorical_encoder: str = 'onehot', n_jobs: int = -1, max_models: Optional[int] = None, progress_callback: Optional[Callable] = None, use_gpu: bool = False, tune: bool = False, tune_top_k: int = 5, tune_trials: int = 50, tune_timeout: Optional[Union[int, float]] = None, tune_backend: str = 'optuna')

Bases: LazyEstimator

Fit all classification algorithms available in scikit-learn and benchmark them.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default verbose (int, optional(default=0))

Set to a positive number to enable progress bars and per-model metric output.

0 ignore_warnings (bool, optional(default=True))

When True, warnings and errors from individual models are suppressed.

True custom_metric (callable or None, optional(default=None))

A function f(y_true, y_pred) used for additional evaluation.

None predictions (bool, optional(default=False))

When True, fit() returns a tuple of (scores, predictions_dataframe).

False random_state (int, optional(default=42))

Random seed passed to models that accept it.

42 classifiers list, str or ``"all"``, optional (default="all")

"all" for every available classifier, or a model name / list of model names and estimator classes to train. Unknown names raise a ValueError.

'all' cv (int or None, optional(default=None))

Number of folds for cross-validation. If None, uses train/test split only.

None timeout (int or float or None, optional(default=None))

Maximum training time in seconds for each model. On POSIX systems, when fit() runs in the main thread, training is interrupted once the limit is reached (code inside C extensions is interrupted when it returns to Python); elsewhere the model is discarded after it finishes. Timed-out models are listed in errors as TimeoutException.

None categorical_encoder (str, optional(default=onehot))

Encoder for categorical features: 'onehot', 'ordinal', 'target', or 'binary'.

'onehot' n_jobs (int, optional(default=-1))

Number of parallel jobs for cross-validation. -1 uses all processors.

-1 max_models (int or None, optional(default=None))

Maximum number of models to train. None means train all.

None progress_callback (callable or None, optional(default=None))

Callback f(model_name, current, total, metrics) called after each model.

None use_gpu (bool, optional(default=False))

When True, enables GPU acceleration.

False tune (bool, optional(default=False))

When True, tunes the top-k models after initial benchmarking.

False tune_top_k (int, optional(default=5))

Number of top models to tune.

5 tune_trials (int, optional(default=50))

Number of optimization trials per model.

50 tune_timeout int, float, or None, optional (default=None)

Maximum seconds per model tuning.

None tune_backend (str, optional(default=optuna))

Tuning backend: 'optuna', 'sklearn', or 'flaml'.

'optuna'

def __init__(
    self,
    verbose: int = 0,
    ignore_warnings: bool = True,
    custom_metric: Optional[Callable] = None,
    predictions: bool = False,
    random_state: int = 42,
    forecasters: Union[str, List[str]] = "all",
    cv: Optional[int] = None,
    timeout: Optional[Union[int, float]] = None,
    n_lags: int = DEFAULT_N_LAGS,
    n_rolling: Tuple[int, ...] = DEFAULT_ROLLING_WINDOWS,
    seasonal_period: Optional[int] = None,
    sort_by: str = DEFAULT_SORT_BY_FORECASTER,
    n_jobs: int = -1,
    max_models: Optional[int] = None,
    progress_callback: Optional[Callable] = None,
    use_gpu: bool = False,
    foundation_model_path: Optional[str] = None,
    # Tuning parameters
    tune: bool = False,
    tune_top_k: int = 5,
    tune_trials: int = 30,
    tune_timeout: Optional[Union[int, float]] = None,
    tune_metric: str = "RMSE",
    tune_seasonal: bool = False,
    # Horizon strategy
    horizon_strategy: str = "recursive",
):
    # Validate
    if cv is not None and (not isinstance(cv, int) or cv < 2):
        raise ValueError(f"cv must be an integer >= 2, got {cv!r}")
    if timeout is not None and (
        not isinstance(timeout, (int, float)) or timeout <= 0
    ):
        raise ValueError(
            f"timeout must be a positive number, got {timeout!r}"
        )
    if custom_metric is not None and not callable(custom_metric):
        raise TypeError(
            f"custom_metric must be callable, got {type(custom_metric)}"
        )
    if max_models is not None and (
        not isinstance(max_models, int) or max_models < 1
    ):
        raise ValueError(
            f"max_models must be a positive integer, got {max_models!r}"
        )
    if tune_metric.upper() not in {"RMSE", "MAE", "MAPE", "SMAPE", "MASE"}:
        raise ValueError(
            f"tune_metric must be one of RMSE, MAE, MAPE, SMAPE, MASE, got {tune_metric!r}"
        )
    if horizon_strategy not in ("recursive", "direct", "multi_output"):
        raise ValueError(
            f"horizon_strategy must be 'recursive', 'direct', or 'multi_output', got {horizon_strategy!r}"
        )
    self._validate_tuning_and_season(tune_top_k, tune_trials, seasonal_period, n_jobs)
    _validate_tune_timeout(tune_timeout)
    sort_by = self._canonical_sort_by(sort_by, custom_metric)
    if sort_by in self._cv_column_names() and not cv:
        raise ValueError(
            f"sort_by={sort_by!r} needs cross-validation: set cv or sort by a test metric"
        )

    self.verbose = verbose
    self.ignore_warnings = ignore_warnings
    self.custom_metric = custom_metric
    self.predictions = predictions
    self.random_state = random_state
    self.forecasters = forecasters
    self.cv = cv
    self.timeout = timeout
    self.n_lags = n_lags
    self.n_rolling = n_rolling
    self.seasonal_period = seasonal_period
    self.sort_by = sort_by
    self.n_jobs = n_jobs
    self.max_models = max_models
    self.progress_callback = progress_callback
    self.use_gpu = use_gpu
    self.foundation_model_path = foundation_model_path
    self.tune = tune
    self.tune_top_k = tune_top_k
    self.tune_trials = tune_trials
    self.tune_timeout = tune_timeout
    self.tune_metric = tune_metric
    self.tune_seasonal = tune_seasonal
    self.horizon_strategy = horizon_strategy
    self.tuned_scores_: Optional[pd.DataFrame] = None
    self.tuned_models_: Dict[str, ForecasterWrapper] = {}

    self.models: Dict[str, ForecasterWrapper] = {}
    self.errors: Dict[str, Exception] = {}
    self._last_predictions: Dict[str, np.ndarray] = {}
    self._validation_cache: Optional[Tuple[Dict[str, np.ndarray], np.ndarray]] = None
    self.mlflow_enabled = setup_mlflow()

def fit(
    self,
    y_train: Union[pd.Series, np.ndarray],
    y_test: Union[pd.Series, np.ndarray],
    X_train: Optional[Union[pd.DataFrame, np.ndarray]] = None,
    X_test: Optional[Union[pd.DataFrame, np.ndarray]] = None,
) -> Tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Fit forecasting models and evaluate on test data.

    Parameters
    ----------
    y_train : array-like
        Training time series (chronological order).
    y_test : array-like
        Held-out future values to forecast against.
    X_train : array-like or None
        Exogenous features for the training period.
    X_test : array-like or None
        Exogenous features for the forecast period.

    Returns
    -------
    scores : pd.DataFrame
        Metric table for every model, sorted by ``sort_by``.
    predictions : pd.DataFrame
        Per-model predictions (empty if ``self.predictions`` is False).
    """
    # Results of a previous fit() must not leak into this one.
    self.models = {}
    self.errors = {}
    self.tuned_scores_ = None
    self.tuned_models_ = {}
    self._last_predictions = {}
    self._validation_cache = None

    test_index = y_test.index if isinstance(y_test, (pd.Series, pd.DataFrame)) else None
    y_train, y_test, X_train, X_test = self._convert_and_validate_inputs(
        y_train, y_test, X_train, X_test
    )
    horizon = len(y_test)
    seasonal_period = self._resolve_seasonal_period(y_train)

    all_forecasters = self._resolve_forecasters(seasonal_period)

    results: List[Dict[str, Any]] = []
    predictions_dict: Dict[str, np.ndarray] = {}

    self._run_all_models(
        all_forecasters, y_train, y_test, X_train, X_test,
        horizon, seasonal_period, results, predictions_dict,
    )

    scores = self._build_scores_dataframe(results)
    self._store_fit_state(
        y_train, y_test, X_train, seasonal_period,
        all_forecasters, predictions_dict, scores,
    )
    self._auto_tune(scores, all_forecasters, y_train, X_train, seasonal_period)

    if self.predictions:
        # Forecast rows keep y_test's index, e.g. its dates.
        return scores, pd.DataFrame(predictions_dict, index=test_index)
    return scores, pd.DataFrame()

def ensemble(
    self,
    method: str = "weighted_average",
    y_true: Optional[np.ndarray] = None,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Combine the test-period forecasts of the fitted models.

    ``"weighted_average"`` and ``"stacking"`` learn from a validation
    window held out from the end of the *training* series: each model is
    refitted on the rest of the training data and forecasts that window.
    Weights are the inverse of those validation RMSEs, and the stacking
    meta-model (Ridge) is fitted on those validation forecasts. The test
    data is never used to build the ensemble.

    Parameters
    ----------
    method : str, optional (default='weighted_average')
        Ensemble method: ``'simple_average'``, ``'weighted_average'``,
        or ``'stacking'``.
    y_true : np.ndarray or None
        Ignored; kept for backward compatibility. (Earlier versions fitted
        the stacking meta-model on the test values passed here, which
        leaked them into the forecast being evaluated.)

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Ensembled predictions for the test period.
    """
    if not self._last_predictions:
        raise ValueError("No predictions available. Call fit() first.")
    if y_true is not None:
        warnings.warn(
            "ensemble(y_true=...) is ignored and will be removed: weights and the "
            "stacking meta-model are now learned on a validation window of the "
            "training series.",
            FutureWarning,
            stacklevel=2,
        )

    handlers = {
        "simple_average": self._ensemble_simple,
        "weighted_average": self._ensemble_weighted,
        "stacking": self._ensemble_stacking,
    }
    handler = handlers.get(method)
    if handler is None:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unknown method: {method}. Use {', '.join(repr(k) for k in handlers)}."
        )
    return np.asarray(handler(self._last_predictions))

    self,
    y_train: Optional[np.ndarray] = None,
    y_test: Optional[np.ndarray] = None,
    plot_type: str = "forecast",
    **kwargs,
):
    """Generate forecast visualizations.

    Parameters
    ----------
    y_train : np.ndarray or None
        Training series. Uses stored values from last ``fit()`` if None.
    y_test : np.ndarray or None
        Test series. Uses stored values from last ``fit()`` if None.
    plot_type : str
        One of ``'forecast'``, ``'comparison'``, ``'residuals'``,
        ``'errors'``, ``'heatmap'``.
    **kwargs
        Passed to the underlying plot function (e.g. ``figsize``,
        ``metric``, ``model_name``, ``top_k``).

    Returns
    -------
    matplotlib.figure.Figure
    """
    y_train = y_train if y_train is not None else getattr(self, "_last_y_train", None)
    y_test = y_test if y_test is not None else getattr(self, "_last_y_test", None)
    predictions = getattr(self, "_last_predictions", {})
    scores = getattr(self, "_last_scores", None)

    handlers = {
        "forecast": self._plot_forecast,
        "comparison": self._plot_comparison,
        "residuals": self._plot_residuals,
        "errors": self._plot_errors,
        "heatmap": self._plot_heatmap,
    }
    handler = handlers.get(plot_type)
    if handler is None:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unknown plot_type: {plot_type!r}. "
            f"Use {', '.join(repr(k) for k in handlers)}."
        )
    return handler(y_train, y_test, predictions, scores, **kwargs)

def diagnose(
    self,
    model_name: Optional[str] = None,
    y_test: Optional[np.ndarray] = None,
):
    """Run residual diagnostics on fitted models.

    Parameters
    ----------
    model_name : str or None
        Specific model name. If None, runs diagnostics for all models
        and returns a DataFrame.
    y_test : np.ndarray or None
        Test values. Uses stored values from last ``fit()`` if None.

    Returns
    -------
    dict or pd.DataFrame
        Single model returns a diagnostic dict; multiple models
        returns a DataFrame with one row per model.
    """
    from lazypredict.ts_diagnostics import compare_diagnostics, residual_diagnostics

    y_test = y_test if y_test is not None else getattr(self, "_last_y_test", None)
    if y_test is None:
        raise ValueError("y_test required. Call fit() first or pass y_test.")

    predictions = getattr(self, "_last_predictions", {})
    if not predictions:
        raise ValueError("No predictions available. Call fit() first.")

    y_train = getattr(self, "_last_y_train", None)
    sp = getattr(self, "_last_seasonal_period", 1) or 1

    if model_name is not None:
        if model_name not in predictions:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Model '{model_name}' not found. "
                f"Available: {list(predictions.keys())}"
            )
        return residual_diagnostics(
            y_test, predictions[model_name],
            y_train=y_train, seasonal_period=sp,
        )

    return compare_diagnostics(
        y_test, predictions,
        y_train=y_train, seasonal_period=sp,
    )

def predict(
    self,
    y_history: Union[pd.Series, np.ndarray],
    horizon: int,
    model_name: Optional[str] = None,
    X_test: Optional[Union[pd.DataFrame, np.ndarray]] = None,
    X_history: Optional[Union[pd.DataFrame, np.ndarray]] = None,
) -> Union[Dict[str, np.ndarray], np.ndarray]:
    """Produce forecasts from previously fitted models.

    A copy of each model is re-fit on ``y_history`` before predicting so
    that the most recent observations are used; the models stored in
    :attr:`models` are left untouched.

    Parameters
    ----------
    y_history : array-like
        Historical time series to condition the forecast on.
    horizon : int
        Number of future time steps to forecast.
    model_name : str or None, optional
        If given, only this model is used and a single ``np.ndarray`` is
        returned.  Otherwise all fitted models are used and a ``dict``
        mapping model names to arrays is returned.
    X_test : array-like or None, optional
        Exogenous features for the ``horizon`` forecast steps.
    X_history : array-like or None, optional
        Exogenous features aligned with ``y_history``. Required, together
        with ``X_test``, when the models were fitted with exogenous
        variables.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray or dict
        A single forecast array when ``model_name`` is specified, or a
        ``{name: np.ndarray}`` dict for all models.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If no models have been fitted, ``model_name`` is not found, or the
        exogenous inputs are missing or misaligned.
    """
    if len(self.models) == 0:
        raise ValueError(
            "No models fitted yet. Call fit() first."
        )
    if model_name is not None and model_name not in self.models:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Model '{model_name}' not found. "
            f"Available: {list(self.models.keys())}"
        )
    if not isinstance(horizon, (int, np.integer)) or horizon < 1:
        raise ValueError(f"horizon must be a positive integer, got {horizon!r}")
    y_history = self._as_series(y_history, "y_history")
    if (X_history is None) != (X_test is None):
        raise ValueError("X_history and X_test must be passed together.")
    if X_history is None and getattr(self, "_last_X_train", None) is not None:
        raise ValueError(
            "The models were fitted with exogenous variables: pass X_history "
            "(aligned with y_history) and X_test (one row per forecast step)."
        )
    if X_history is not None:
        X_history = self._as_exog(X_history, "X_history", len(y_history), "y_history")
        X_test = self._as_exog(X_test, "X_test", horizon, "the forecast horizon")

    names = [model_name] if model_name is not None else list(self.models)
    result = {}
    for name in names:
        wrapper = copy.deepcopy(self.models[name])
        wrapper.fit(y_history, X_history)
        result[name] = np.asarray(wrapper.predict(horizon, X_test), dtype=float)
    if model_name is not None:
        return result[model_name]
    return result

def save_models(self, path: str) -> None:
    """Save all fitted models to disk using ``joblib``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    path : str
        Directory path.  Created if it does not exist.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If no models have been fitted yet.
    """
    import os

    import joblib

    if len(self.models) == 0:
        raise ValueError("No models fitted yet. Call fit() first.")
    os.makedirs(path, exist_ok=True)
    for name, wrapper in self.models.items():
        filepath = os.path.join(path, f"{name}.joblib")
        joblib.dump(wrapper, filepath)
        logger.info("Saved %s to %s", name, filepath)

def load_models(self, path: str) -> Dict[str, ForecasterWrapper]:
    """Load previously saved models from disk.

    Parameters
    ----------
    path : str
        Directory containing ``.joblib`` files written by
        :meth:`save_models`.

    Returns
    -------
    dict
        Mapping of model name to :class:`ForecasterWrapper`.

    Raises
    ------
    FileNotFoundError
        If ``path`` does not exist.
    """
    import os

    import joblib

    if not os.path.isdir(path):
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Directory not found: {path}")
    for filename in os.listdir(path):
        if filename.endswith(".joblib"):
            name = filename[:-7]
            filepath = os.path.join(path, filename)
            self.models[name] = joblib.load(filepath)
            logger.info("Loaded %s from %s", name, filepath)
    return self.models
